newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU gas oil users get some comfort from stocks data.
newsitem.headline: EU gas oil users get some comfort from stocks data.

text.p: The larger than expected build in distillate stocks should provide gas oil buyers with a little comfort, but still leaves the market tight and particularly vulnerable if the weather turns cold, analysts said on Tuesday.

"It's a fairly decent sort of build and it will take some of the pressure off..., but, unless we have unusually mild weather, it will still be tight at the end of the year," said UBS energy economist Geoff Pyne.

Middle distillate stocks in the European Union, excluding Sweden, rose 6.60 million barrels, or 2.3 percent, in October to 291.45 million barrels, thus reducing the year-on-year shortfall by 11.82 million barrels, Stitching Euroilstock said in its latest monthly report.
Analysts, however, preferred to look at the simple year-on-year comparison. Distillate stocks were still 21.65 million barrels lower than at the end of October 1995.
"We're still at a very low level. We're very much down on last year which wasn't particularly high," said Mike Barry of Energy Market Consultants (EMC).
"If (the weather) is fairly normal, it's still tight, but not a major crisis, but it's certainly not clear blue water until the end of winter," said Lesley Owens, analyst at Petroleum Economics.
Most analysts expected a slight growth in gas oil stocks, although the size of the build surprised most.
Supply improved with a rise of cargo imports from the United States, the former Soviet Union, and an incentive within Europe to produce gas oil, particularly low sulphur material.
"We understand some 120,000 bpd (barrels per day) was coming out of the U.S, the majority of it low sulphur," said Owens.
Demand was also down, noticeably in Germany, as high prices discouraged buying.
"There was a noticeable build in Germany due, we believe, to the low sales (to end-users)...We also suspect they have been buying in the past few days," said Barry.
The gas oil build also contributed to the fall in IPE gas oil futures in mid-afternoon. The December contract dropped $3 shortly after the release of the figures as bearish sentiment hit.
"The market's going to dive on these," said one trader at the time.
Futures subsequently recovered, but dealers still said the market was vulnerable to further losses. According to one trader, the news had taken "some of the sting out of the market."
Crude stocks, meanwhile, were hardly changed, down a mere 80,000 barrels to 401.06 million barrels.
"Crude was not as helpful as it might have been. A build would clearly have taken more pressure off," said UBS's Pyne.
